title: Music Licensing for Fitness Apps and On-Demand Classes

body_markdown:
A fitness app can turn one instructor-led workout into a livestream, an on-demand replay, an offline download and a promotional clip. Each version can change the music licensing requirements. Permission to play songs in a physical studio does not automatically authorize distributing those songs inside a subscription app.


For platforms, labels and publishers, the practical challenge is matching the rights granted to the product actually being built. A deal that covers streamed class videos may leave downloads, audio-only coaching or social advertising outside its scope.


This guide takes a U.S.-focused approach to clearing fitness content, structuring commercial terms and keeping a growing class library within its permissions. International availability requires additional territorial review.


## The rights a fitness class can involve


A commercial recording usually involves two separate copyrights: the musical composition and the sound recording. The publisher or songwriter may control the composition, while a label, artist or another owner controls the recording. Ownership and licensing authority must be confirmed for each side.


The[U.S. Copyright Act identifies separate exclusive rights](https://www.copyright.gov/title17/92chap1.html#106) , including reproduction, distribution and public performance. A fitness platform should not assume that permission addressing one right resolves the others.


For an app-based workout library, music licensing typically requires reviewing the following layers:


Rights layer


Relevant fitness use


Typical clearance route


Composition synchronization


Pairing a composition with recorded workout video


Publisher, songwriter or authorized licensing representative


Master use


Including a particular recording in the workout


Label, recording owner or authorized representative


Composition public performance


Streaming or otherwise publicly performing compositions


Relevant performing rights organizations, direct licensors or a combination


Reproduction and download permissions


Creating authorized copies, including offline class files


Applicable composition and recording rights holders, with audiovisual use expressly addressed


Audio-only rights


Offering guided runs, music-led audio workouts or standalone listening


A separate analysis of composition and recording permissions


These categories can overlap within a negotiated agreement. What matters is the actual grant, not whether the document is called a catalog license, platform agreement or content partnership. For foundational context, the distinction between[composition, master and performance permissions](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/law-license-basics-how-modern-music-licenses-actually-work) helps explain why several parties may need to approve one track.


## Match permissions to the delivery format


### Livestreams and on-demand replays


Start by separating a genuinely live transmission from a recorded class that remains available afterward. The same instructor session can create different uses when the platform records it, edits it and adds it to a searchable library.


A livestream should not be treated as exempt from clearance simply because viewers cannot replay it. Review the applicable performance rights and obtain permissions appropriate to the audiovisual transmission, including any recording or copying involved in production and delivery.


Music licensing for an on-demand library should expressly cover recording music into classes, hosting those classes and making them available when subscribers choose. A live-only agreement should not be stretched to cover unlimited replays.


Also distinguish the instructor’s premises from the distribution service. A venue’s public-performance arrangement may address music played in the room without clearing the app’s transmission or recorded content.


### Offline downloads and audio-only workouts


Offline access introduces copies on user devices. Specify whether downloads are permitted, how long they remain playable and what happens when a subscription or track license expires. Product teams should confirm that the app can implement those restrictions.


Audio-only workouts deserve their own review. A guided run with selectable tracks is not necessarily licensed on the same basis as a fixed workout video.


The[statutory digital audio framework](https://www.copyright.gov/title17/92chap1.html#114) is not blanket authorization for interactive listening or audiovisual classes. Likewise, a composition mechanical license does not, by itself, clear synchronization with video or use of a particular master recording. The Mechanical Licensing Collective’s digital service resources explain its role in eligible digital audio uses, which should not be confused with audiovisual clearance.


Avoid describing a product merely as “streaming fitness.” List the actual formats and user controls so licensors can assess them.


## Choose a catalog strategy that fits the workout experience


Familiar commercial tracks can be central to an instructor’s programming, but they may require negotiations across several owners. Production music, directly licensed independent catalogs and commissioned recordings offer other routes. None should be assumed to include every fitness use automatically.


A workable music licensing strategy starts with the experience the platform needs to deliver. A cycling service built around recognizable songs has different requirements from a meditation app using unobtrusive instrumental beds.


Evaluate candidate catalogs against three questions:


-


**Workout suitability:** Does the repertoire support the required tempo, duration, energy and lyrical standards?


-


**Clearance authority:** Can the licensor authorize both composition and recording uses, or must another party approve?


-


**Operational flexibility:** Does the agreement permit the intended editing, delivery formats, territories and class availability?


“Royalty-free” describes a licensing arrangement, not an absence of copyright. Check restrictions on subscription products, standalone music access, downloadable content and promotional use.


Commissioned music also needs written terms. Address ownership or license scope, contributor permissions, permitted adaptations and delivery of usable stems. Paying a producer’s invoice does not necessarily transfer every relevant right.


For rights holders, a focused catalog offer can be more useful than unrestricted access to a large repertoire. Accurate ownership data and clear permissions reduce the time needed to approve suitable tracks.


## Budget around usage, not a universal per-song price


There is no universal rate for licensing a song in a fitness app. Quotes depend on the track, rights controlled, territories, duration, audience, delivery methods and negotiating context.


For music licensing budgets, separate the upfront cost of access from the cost of growth. A small launch library can become expensive if the agreement charges for each new class, replay or active subscriber without a workable forecasting model.


Potential commercial structures include fixed fees, minimum guarantees, revenue shares, usage-based royalties or combinations of these. The agreement should define the calculation precisely rather than relying on labels such as “per stream.”


A stream might mean a class started, a track played or a qualifying amount of listening. Those definitions produce different invoices. Similarly, a revenue share needs an agreed revenue base, treatment of bundled subscriptions and any permitted deductions.


Model several operating scenarios before accepting terms. Include ordinary growth, a successful launch and a class that becomes unusually popular. Test free trials, discounted subscriptions, corporate memberships and repeat viewing.


For rights holders, the same exercise reveals whether compensation tracks actual exploitation. Reporting obligations and audit provisions matter as much as the headline percentage when payment depends on platform activity.


## Negotiate the permissions that product teams will actually use


### Territories, term and continued class availability


A license should identify where users may access content, not just where the platform is incorporated. If rights are limited to particular countries, agree on the territorial controls and travel-related access rules the service will apply.


Music licensing terms should also distinguish the period for creating new classes from the period for distributing existing ones. Those periods need not be identical.


For example, a platform might request permission to produce classes during a defined production window and retain those approved classes for a separately negotiated period. That arrangement exists only if the rights holder agrees to it.


Address expiry early: whether classes must disappear immediately, whether a limited run-off is allowed and how offline copies become unavailable. Do not leave a permanent archive implied by silence.


### Editing, instructor interaction and promotional extracts


Workout production commonly involves fading tracks, shortening introductions, looping passages or adjusting timing. Describe the intended edits and obtain the necessary permissions. A general right to include a song should not be treated as approval for every alteration.


Instructor voice-over, lyric display, translated lyrics and audience sing-alongs can raise separate questions. Flag these features during clearance rather than after production.


Promotion also needs a defined scope. A class license may not authorize paid advertisements, app-store previews or influencer posts containing the soundtrack. The issues around[music in influencer campaigns](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/influencer-campaign-music-who-needs-a-license-and-when) become relevant when instructors or partners republish workout excerpts.


A short promotional extract is still a separate use to evaluate, especially when it leaves the licensed app.


### Ownership assurances and catalog changes


Strong music licensing agreements identify what the licensor controls and how changes to that control will be communicated. For compositions, establish whether all necessary interests are covered or whether additional publisher approvals remain outstanding.


An ISRC identifies a recording, but it does not prove that the party offering it controls every requested right. Likewise, a song title alone is insufficient to distinguish recordings, remixes or versions.


Agree on a process for disputed ownership, withdrawn tracks and expired permissions. It should specify notice, response times, affected uses and the treatment of previously approved classes.


Platforms need a practical replacement process; rights holders need confidence that withdrawal instructions reach every relevant distribution surface. Neither objective is served by a contract that requires removal without identifying which assets contain the track.


## Build a music licensing workflow before launch


Clearance should become part of class production rather than a final legal check after filming. Once an instructor has choreographed a session around an unavailable track, replacement becomes a production problem as well as a legal one.


A reliable workflow connects the proposed playlist to the final published asset. Assign one person or team responsibility for confirming that permissions match the intended release.


Use a consistent sequence:


-


**Define the use:** Record the class format, territories, availability period, download settings and planned promotion.


-


**Verify the track:** Confirm the recording version, identifiers, ownership interests and licensing contacts.


-


**Document approval:** Retain executed agreements, track schedules, restrictions and any required creative approvals.


-


**Check the final class:** Compare the actual music, edits and duration against what was cleared.


-


**Control publication:** Publish only approved versions and connect expiry dates to removal or renewal tasks.


Treat music licensing records as production data. A restriction stored only in an email attachment is easy for an editor or release manager to miss.


Consider a 45-minute cycling class that uses several songs, includes an offline option and generates a short advertising clip. The clearance record should connect those outputs to the relevant permissions. Approval for the streamed class should not silently become approval for the download and advertisement.


Keep editable production files and, where feasible, separate music from instructor audio. That makes replacement possible without automatically reshooting the entire session.


## Make usage reporting useful to both sides


Usage-based deals work best when commercial definitions map to events the app can actually measure. Legal, finance and engineering teams should agree on reporting requirements before signature.


At minimum, the reporting specification should identify tracks and classes, reporting periods, relevant territories and the activity used to calculate payment. Depending on the deal, that activity may include class plays, track plays, listening duration, downloads or subscriber counts.


Music licensing reports should distinguish these measures rather than combining them into an undefined engagement figure. A user opening a class is not necessarily the same event as hearing every track in it.


For rights holders, request enough information to reconcile royalties and identify unexpected uses. For platforms, avoid promising data that cannot be captured reliably or shared consistently with privacy obligations.


Set reporting deadlines, correction procedures, record-retention periods and appropriate audit rights. Explain how missing or revised data affects an invoice.


Reporting should also support compliance beyond payment. A class-to-track register lets teams find affected videos when rights expire, identify which offline assets need disabling and check whether promotional exports remain authorized.


## Frequently asked questions


**Does a gym’s music license cover its fitness app?** Not automatically. A license for music played at physical premises should not be assumed to cover livestreams, recorded classes, downloads or advertising. Review the actual grant and obtain the additional permissions required for the digital service.


**Can instructors use songs from a personal streaming subscription?** A consumer subscription generally provides listening access under that service’s terms, not permission to incorporate recordings into commercial workout content. Music licensing for the fitness product must be addressed separately from how an instructor discovers or listens to songs.


**Is music under 30 seconds automatically permitted?** No. U.S. copyright law has no general rule making short music excerpts automatically free to use. Duration alone does not establish permission or fair use, and an excerpt in an advertisement or workout still needs a use-specific assessment.


**Does a performing rights organization license clear the whole class?** No. An applicable composition public-performance license does not, by itself, grant composition synchronization rights or permission to use a particular recording. Confirm repertoire coverage and the additional rights required by the class format.


**What does it cost to license a song for a fitness app?** There is no standard price. Request a quote describing the recording, class formats, audience, territories, term, downloads and promotional uses. Compare the total projected cost across realistic growth scenarios rather than comparing upfront fees alone.


## Start with a clearance-ready class plan


Before requesting quotes or offering a catalog, prepare a concise use specification: what users can watch or hear, where they can access it, how long it stays available and what the business will report.


That document gives music licensing negotiations a concrete starting point. Platforms can price and build against defined permissions, while labels and publishers can evaluate compensation, control and operational risk. The goal is a class library whose contracts, production practices and product features all describe the same use.
